title: Bank NXT Migrates ATM and Debit Card Portfolio to Network International
snippet: Egypt's Bank NXT is moving its ATM and debit card processing to Network International's end-to-end platform as part of a broader The post Bank NXT Migrates ATM and Debit Card Portfolio to Network International appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Bank NXT, the Egyptian retail and corporate lender majority-owned by EFG Holding, has extended its processing relationship with Network International, migrating its ATM and debit card portfolio to the Dubai-headquartered firm’s end-to-end platform. The announcement, made in Cairo on 12 October 2026, positions the move as a core component of Bank NXT’s infrastructure modernisation programme, with the stated goals of tightening security controls and accelerating the rollout of new digital services.

Tamer Seif El-Din, CEO and managing director at Bank NXT

The bank, formerly known as aiBANK, operates 37 branches across Egypt and has been expanding its ATM network. Its paid-up capital stood at EGP 9.9 billion following a board-approved cash increase in August 2025. EFG Holding holds a 51 per cent stake, with Egypt’s Financial Services and Digital Transformation Sub-Fund holding 25 per cent and the National Investment Bank holding 24 per cent.

Tamer Seif El-Din, chief executive and managing director of Bank NXT, said the migration would allow the bank to introduce new services more quickly and support its expansion agenda. “Migrating our debit card and ATM portfolio to Network’s robust processing platform will enable us to achieve greater operational efficiency, introduce innovative services faster, and ultimately, provide a secure and digitally advanced banking experience,” he said.

Egypt’s digital payments push

The partnership sits within a deliberate national policy context. The Central Bank of Egypt has made payments digitalisation a formal priority, pushing financial institutions to modernise legacy infrastructure and broaden electronic payment acceptance. Egypt’s relatively young population, high mobile penetration and a large unbanked segment make the country one of the more consequential emerging markets for payment infrastructure investment in the Africa and Middle East region.

Network International operates across more than 50 countries and counts more than 250 financial institutions among its processing clients. Dr Reda Helal, group managing director for processing, Africa and growth markets at Network, described the deal as part of a broader strategy to deepen the firm’s footprint across the MEA region. The company was taken private following its 2023 acquisition by a consortium led by Brookfield Asset Management and Francisco Partners, removing it from the London Stock Exchange where it had traded since 2019. That ownership structure gives it access to capital for platform investment that publicly listed peers must justify quarter-by-quarter.

Competitive and regulatory read-across

End-to-end card processing is a competitive and commoditised segment, with regional and global players including Fiserv, FIS and Mastercard‘s processing arm competing for bank outsourcing mandates alongside regional specialists. The commercial logic for an Egyptian mid-tier bank is straightforward: outsourcing ATM and debit card processing to a specialist avoids the capital expenditure and ongoing technology maintenance of running proprietary switching infrastructure, while giving access to updated fraud and security tooling that regulators increasingly expect.

The next milestones to watch are the pace of migration, whether Bank NXT pursues further infrastructure partnerships as it opens new branches, and how the Central Bank of Egypt’s ongoing digitalisation agenda shapes procurement decisions across the wider Egyptian banking sector.

title: MiCA at 100 days: Euro Stablecoins Rise as OTC Flows Diverge
snippet: A joint institutional review finds euro stablecoin supply up 23% post-MiCA, while OTC crypto volumes grew 57% as centralised exchanges contracted. The post MiCA at 100 days: Euro Stablecoins Rise as OTC Flows Diverge appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
One hundred days after the close of MiCA’s transitional period on 1 July 2026, a multi-contributor market review published by Finery Markets, alongside Banking Circle, Fipto, The Vault and Sumsub, sets out how the regulation is reshaping digital asset trading, stablecoin issuance, custody and compliance across the EU.

The report draws on more than 16 million institutional spot crypto trades executed on Finery Markets’ platform in the first nine months of 2026, compared with the same period of 2025.

OTC diverges from exchange markets

The headline trading finding is a sharp split between institutional OTC venues and centralised exchanges. Finery Markets’ OTC spot volume grew 57% year on year in the nine months to September 2026, while the top-20 centralised exchanges contracted 47% and the top-20 decentralised exchanges fell 35% over the same period. OTC volume grew in every month of 2026; centralised exchange volume was down year on year in every month.

Finery Markets managing director Sergey Klinkov attributes the divergence to structural factors familiar from the evolution of FX markets: large-block institutional flow gravitates to OTC rails for execution discretion, lower market impact and capital efficiency. The analogy the firm draws is to MiFID II, which concentrated equities and fixed-income execution in institutional-grade infrastructure as compliance costs squeezed sub-scale brokers out of the market. Klinkov expects MiCA to produce a similar consolidation in crypto, pushing smaller operators to merge or exit.

Within non-stablecoin OTC flow, the composition shifted markedly. Ethereum’s share of non-stablecoin volume rose from 23% in the first nine months of 2025 to 50% in the same period of 2026, a 222% increase in absolute volume terms, while Bitcoin’s share fell from 48% to 29% and its volume declined 13%.

Euro stablecoin supply grows from a small base

Stablecoins accounted for 83% of trades on the Finery Markets platform, with stablecoin volume up 76% year on year. Euro-linked stablecoins are the fastest-growing segment, though the absolute scale remains modest. EURC volume on the platform rose 46-fold year on year, yet still represents only 0.12% of stablecoin client flows. On-chain, euro-stablecoin supply reached $848 million by early September 2026, up 22.6% from $692 million at the start of the year, according to Token Terminal. Dollar-linked stablecoin supply, by comparison, stood at roughly $299 billion, broadly flat over the same period.

Fipto chief executive Patrick Mollard frames the supply growth as a structural shift rather than a displacement of dollar liquidity. He notes that a growing share of demand for euro-denominated stablecoins is coming from payment companies in Canada, Africa and Asia-Pacific seeking a regulated euro leg they can hold, redeem at par and reconcile under European rules. He also observes that many firms that missed the 1 July CASP authorisation deadline have not left the market; the compliant path has been to partner with a licensed CASP that carries the regulatory responsibility.

Reserve caps and compliance friction

Banking Circle head of legal Ida Mokhtassi highlights the EBA’s “double test” on reserve concentration as a practical burden for issuers. Under current rules, a stablecoin issuer placing €1 billion of reserves with smaller credit institutions faces a 5% cap per bank, requiring at least 20 banking relationships; the 1.5% total-assets test tightens that further. Banking Circle’s position is that the concentration limits should be calibrated to the quality of the safeguard rather than the size of the bank. “Reserves held in a bankruptcy-remote structure are protected whatever the size of the bank holding them,” Mokhtassi writes, arguing the double test should not apply where ring-fenced, readily available liquidity directly addresses the EBA’s concern.

Sumsub legal counsel Egor Larichkin adds a compliance operations note: EU crypto verifications fell by almost 13% quarter on quarter following the deadline, with sharp contractions in Germany and Belgium. Simultaneously, the share of EU crypto applicants rejected for fraud attempts rose by almost half, more than twice the increase seen elsewhere. Larichkin attributes this to fraudsters exploiting platform re-onboarding processes, targeting users confused by migration to new legal entities with fake re-verification requests.

Regulatory read-across

MiCA’s first hundred days sit inside a broader EU regulatory stack. PSD2 creates overlapping authorisation requirements for e-money token transfers, and The Vault chief executive Artem Stopnevich notes that a MiCA licence alone does not cover every activity needed to operate a complete payment service. The resolution to that overlap, whether through EBA guidance or targeted legislative refinement under any future PSD3 review, will determine how smoothly stablecoin payment rails connect to existing payment institution infrastructure. For now, the commercial incentive runs toward partnership rather than parallel licensing.

title: Gibraltar Signs MOU with ADI Foundation on Stablecoin Consortium
snippet: Gibraltar and ADI Foundation will explore a sterling, dollar and euro stablecoin consortium built on ADI Chain for institutional cross-border settlement. The post Gibraltar Signs MOU with ADI Foundation on Stablecoin Consortium appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Gibraltar’s government and Abu Dhabi-based ADI Foundation have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore creating a multi-currency stablecoin consortium, with digital currencies referenced to sterling, the US dollar and the euro. The announcement marks an early-stage commitment rather than a live product: issuance remains contingent on commercial viability, the recruitment of founding members drawn from Gibraltar-licensed institutions, and full regulatory authorisation.

Under the proposed structure, each currency would be issued through a separate entity, with reserves held one-for-one in high-quality liquid assets denominated in the corresponding reference currency. Reserves would be independently attested and subject to annual audit. ADI Foundation would provide issuance infrastructure through ADI Chain, which the foundation describes as the GCC and MENA region’s first sovereign digital infrastructure built for governments and institutions.

The regulatory and structural angle

Gibraltar’s involvement carries some credibility in the distributed ledger technology space. The territory introduced a purpose-built regulatory framework for DLT businesses in 2018, making it an early mover among common law jurisdictions. The government has since added a bespoke prediction market regime and legislation facilitating tokenised fund shares and DLT-based share registers. Minister for Justice, Trade and Industry Nigel Feetham KC MP said the stablecoin project builds on that legislative track record and forms part of a nine-month international outreach programme aimed at attracting digital-finance investment.

ADI Chain already acts as settlement infrastructure for DDSC, a dirham-backed stablecoin initiated by IHC, Sirius International Holding and First Abu Dhabi Bank, which holds a licence from the UAE Central Bank. That live deployment gives ADI Foundation a reference architecture for reserve management and institutional issuance, though operating sterling- and euro-referenced instruments in European regulatory perimeters introduces a separate compliance layer. The EU’s Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation, which came into force progressively from 2024, sets out specific requirements for e-money tokens and asset-referenced tokens, and any euro-denominated issuance targeting EU counterparties will need to navigate that framework carefully.

Market context

The broader institutional stablecoin segment is maturing quickly. Several consortia and sovereign-adjacent projects are competing to become the settlement layer connecting payments corridors across Europe, the Middle East and Africa. Fnality International, backed by a group of global banks, has been building sterling and dollar payment system assets for wholesale settlement. JPMorgan‘s Kinexys network and the BIS Project mBridge have demonstrated cross-border settlement use cases at scale. The Gibraltar-ADI project’s stated long-term ambition, connecting Europe and Africa through the AfCFTA digital trade infrastructure that ADI is developing with the African Continental Free Trade Area Secretariat, addresses a corridor that is structurally underserved by existing correspondent banking rails but also one where regulatory fragmentation across dozens of jurisdictions is a genuine execution risk.

Ajay Bhatia, Principal Council Member at ADI Foundation, said the project’s ambition is “to explore building a regulated financial infrastructure that allows digital money to move seamlessly between institutions, markets and economies”, adding that Gibraltar brings DLT experience while ADI brings infrastructure and an international network.

The parties will also assess whether consortium management, operations and compliance functions should be based in Gibraltar, which would affect licensing obligations and the jurisdiction’s capacity to supervise a multi-currency issuer. The next concrete milestones to watch are the identity of founding bank members and the regulatory pathway chosen for the sterling instrument, where the Bank of England’s evolving stablecoin regime will be the primary gating factor.

title: Convera Names Four C-Suite Hires to Build Global Payments Platform
snippet: The commercial payments firm has appointed a new COO, CTO, CPO and CIO to drive its integrated cross-border money movement roadmap. The post Convera Names Four C-Suite Hires to Build Global Payments Platform appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Convera has announced four senior leadership appointments as it pushes to consolidate its cross-border payments, FX risk management and multi-currency capabilities into a single integrated platform. Mike Cahill joins as EVP and Chief Operating Officer, Jon Southall as SVP and Chief Technology Officer, Tui Allen as SVP and Chief Product Officer, and Chris Steinig as Chief Information Officer.

The four hires collectively oversee Convera’s combined product, technology and operations organisation, a structural alignment that signals the company is moving from a functionally siloed model toward a more unified delivery capability. Cahill, who had been serving as Interim Chief Product and Technology Officer since joining in June 2026, now takes permanent operational responsibility across all three functions.

The appointments in detail

Southall arrives from PayPal, where he managed the Large Enterprise Platform handling more than $1.5 trillion in annual transaction volume. His background at Boku and Braintree adds further high-volume infrastructure experience. Allen comes from Ticketmaster/Live Nation and Shopify, bringing product design and adoption experience that is less typical for a B2B payments firm but relevant as Convera courts fintechs and business platforms seeking embedded FX and payments capabilities. Steinig is an internal promotion: a 25-year Convera veteran who will focus on platform modernisation and operational resilience.

Group chief executive Patrick Gauthier framed the hires around a problem the company believes remains structurally unsolved in commercial cross-border payments. “Businesses don’t just need faster or less expensive cross-border payments. They need to know where their money is, what it is worth and how to protect it as it moves,” he said.

Cahill added that the team’s near-term priority is disciplined execution rather than product invention. “Our focus is disciplined execution: translating customer needs into products, modernising the technology that supports them and delivering consistently in every market we serve,” he said.

Market context

Convera operates in a segment that has attracted significant capital and consolidation pressure over the past several years. The company processes close to $200 billion in annual payment flows across more than 140 currencies and 200 countries and territories, a regulatory and network footprint that few pure-play fintechs have matched. Its principal competitors in the enterprise and mid-market cross-border space include specialist firms such as Corpay and Western Union Business Solutions, as well as bank treasury services and a growing tier of API-first challengers including Airwallex, Wise Business and Nium.

The strategic direction Convera has outlined, combining payment execution with embedded FX hedging and multi-currency account holding at the point of transaction, reflects a broader industry shift. As businesses demand treasury-adjacent functionality from their payments providers rather than maintaining separate banking, FX and treasury relationships, the ability to offer an integrated ledger becomes a structural differentiator rather than a feature.

The appointment of a CPO with consumer-grade product experience is notable in that context. B2B cross-border payments have historically prioritised reliability and compliance over user experience; the combination of Allen’s background with Southall’s infrastructure depth suggests Convera is targeting both dimensions simultaneously.

The next indicators to watch will be product releases against the Multi-Currency Account and API roadmap Convera has previously signalled, and whether the new leadership team accelerates any commercial partnership announcements with banks or embedded-finance platforms in the near term.

title: Capsafa Launches Free Financial Life Organiser for UK Households
snippet: The self-funded fintech startup aims to help households track accounts, pensions and policies, with broker and adviser partnerships as its planned growth engine. The post Capsafa Launches Free Financial Life Organiser for UK Households appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Capsafa, a UK fintech startup founded by financial services technology entrepreneur Dan Yorke, launched in September 2026 with a free platform designed to help households consolidate records of their accounts, investments, pensions, insurance policies and property in one place. The product is self-funded and the core service, including an Executor Pack that summarises a user’s recorded financial affairs, is positioned as permanently free.

Dan Yorke, founder and CEO at Capsafa

Yorke, who has worked in financial services technology since 1998 and runs a mortgage and business finance brokerage, said he built the platform after repeatedly watching missing paperwork delay client applications. “Every provider gives its customers a view of the product they hold with them,” he said. “But keeping track of how it all fits together is still largely the customers’ job. As they change jobs, move house and take out new policies, it becomes increasingly difficult to manage.”

The platform does not connect directly to financial accounts or require login credentials. Instead, users upload documents manually or note where originals are held, and set renewal and review reminders. Data is encrypted in transit and at rest using AES-256 encryption, two-factor authentication is compulsory on every login, and the company says it does not sell user data. Before launch, Capsafa underwent penetration testing by AppSecure Security, a CREST-approved firm, and holds UK government-backed Cyber Essentials certification.

Capsafa commissioned a OnePoll survey, covering savings accounts, investments and debts, which found that 25% of UK adults were not confident their family could locate and understand all of their financial affairs without their help. The company is using that figure to frame the commercial case for its organiser.

The partnership model

The go-to-market strategy is built on professional distribution rather than direct consumer acquisition. Capsafa is actively seeking partnerships with mortgage brokers, financial advisers, accountants and will-writing firms, which it expects will introduce the organiser to clients at moments when financial organisation is already front of mind, such as a remortgage or an estate-planning review. Revenue is planned through optional premium features and commercial partnership arrangements, though no pricing or partner names have been disclosed at this stage.

The model is notable in a market where open banking and account-aggregation platforms have, for several years, competed for the same household-organisation use case. Products from established providers in the aggregation space typically require API-based connections to financial institutions, pulling live balances and transaction data. Capsafa takes a deliberately lighter approach: a manual, document-centric organiser that explicitly avoids holding account credentials or acting as a financial aggregator. That distinction may reduce regulatory surface area but also limits the real-time utility the platform can offer compared with connected alternatives.

Market context

The UK financial wellbeing and household-organisation segment has attracted several entrants, from open-banking-powered apps to legacy financial-planning tools. The differentiator Capsafa is betting on is simplicity of compliance posture and the professional intermediary channel. By not aggregating live financial data, it sits outside the directly supervised perimeter for account information services under UK Payment Services Regulations, which could lower the regulatory cost of onboarding broker and adviser distribution partners.

The immediate question is whether professional partners will integrate the referral into their client journey consistently enough to build household adoption at scale. Capsafa does not yet have named partners on record, and the self-funded model means the runway for that distribution effort is constrained until premium revenue or partnership fees begin to materialise.

title: Bybit Adds Stock Trading and Tokenised Equities in TradFi push
snippet: The Dubai crypto exchange has launched US stock trading and is developing tokenised shares with Mantle, as it pursues a broader financial platform strategy. The post Bybit Adds Stock Trading and Tokenised Equities in TradFi push appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Bybit has launched trading in more than 1,000 US stocks and exchange-traded funds, and is developing a tokenised equity product called mStocks in collaboration with Mantle, as the Dubai-headquartered exchange accelerates its expansion beyond crypto markets. Chief executive Ben Zhou outlined the plans at the company’s biannual “Keynote with Ben” session on 14 October.

Ben Zhou, co-founder and CEO at ByBit

The stock trading product, which went live on 12 October, allows eligible users to buy and sell US equities using USDC, with fractional share support and 24-hour, five-day access that covers pre-market, regular and after-hours sessions. The product sits within Bybit’s existing Unified Trading Account, which already supports crypto derivatives and foreign exchange.

mStocks and the tokenised equity layer

The more structurally novel move is mStocks, which Bybit is targeting for a November launch. The product is described as a tokenised stock backed one-to-one by real underlying securities, with planned support for round-the-clock conversion between eligible stocks and mStocks. Converted tokens would also be usable as collateral within the Unified Trading Account and tradeable through automated market maker liquidity pools on the Mantle network.

Bybit also offers IPO Express, launched in June, which gives eligible users access to selected initial public offering opportunities at the offering price through tokenised representations. The company said the service launched with SpaceX as the first available offering, extending its reach from secondary to selected primary markets.

The company says its TradFi perpetuals business has recorded more than 180 billion dollars in cumulative trading volume since it entered CFD markets in 2022, and its catalogue now spans more than 600 instruments across equities, indices, commodities and FX. It has also launched Forex Perps and Perp Options, a derivatives structure it describes as industry-first, built on top of TradFi perpetuals rather than spot prices.

Regulatory and competitive context

The regulatory backdrop for this model is complex. Tokenised securities fall under securities law in most jurisdictions, and cross-border platforms face fragmented licensing requirements. Bybit said it secured five new licences and regulatory approvals during 2026, across the European Union, the Cayman Islands, Indonesia, South Africa and El Salvador, though it did not name the specific licence categories or the product lines they cover. That ambiguity matters: whether mStocks constitutes a security, a derivative or a stablecoin-adjacent instrument will determine where it can be offered and under which disclosure regime.

Several competitors are pursuing adjacent strategies. Robinhood has moved to extend its crypto and equities offering across European markets, while Coinbase has flagged interest in expanding into derivatives and equities products for international users. Traditional prime brokers and retail platforms including Interactive Brokers have meanwhile integrated crypto custody and trading alongside conventional equities, compressing the differentiation Bybit seeks. The exchange’s distinctive angle is the collateral interoperability between crypto and stock positions within a single account structure, a feature that has real appeal for active traders but that also raises margin and risk management questions regulators will scrutinise closely.

Bybit also said it intercepted more than 30,000 suspicious withdrawal requests in the first half of 2026, representing more than 700 million dollars in protected assets, and launched Bybit AI in September as a conversational assistant across trading, account management and customer support.

Ben Zhou framed the direction in broad terms: “We have brought trading, investing, payments and AI together, and we are continuing to add more markets and more ways to use them.”

The company says its Bybit Card and Bybit Pay services now reach more than 5,000 merchants across more than 15 countries, with more than four million cards issued. The payments infrastructure appears designed to extend platform stickiness beyond the trading session, though the commercial model for the card programme and the unit economics of the merchant network were not disclosed.

The next markers to watch are the jurisdictions in which mStocks launches, the regulatory classification Bybit receives for the product, and whether the IPO Express pre-market offering expands beyond its initial single-issuer format.

title: SoDEX Adds Morpho-Powered USDC Lending Yield via Unified Labs
snippet: ValueChain's SoDEX platform has integrated Morpho's open credit network, letting users deposit USDC into curated vaults to earn on-chain lending yield. The post SoDEX Adds Morpho-Powered USDC Lending Yield via Unified Labs appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
ValueChain‘s SoDEX trading and wealth application has integrated Morpho, the on-chain credit network that reported more than $16 billion in deposits as of October 2026. The integration allows SoDEX users to deposit USDC into a Morpho Vault curated by Unified Labs, earning yield generated by borrowing activity across the markets to which the vault allocates. The product is live now at sodex.com/wealth.

The vault’s allocation policy, collateral parameters and risk limits are set by Unified Labs, which describes itself as Asia’s first institutional-grade risk curator focused on the intersection of real-world assets and decentralised finance. Deposits and redemptions are handled within the SoDEX interface, removing the need for a separate wallet connection or a standalone DeFi workflow.

How the product works

The earn product sits inside SoDEX Wealth and is enabled by the ValueChain-Base bridge, which routes stablecoin deposits from ValueChain’s layer-one blockchain onto the Base network where the Morpho Vault operates. Yield accrues from borrowing demand rather than from token emissions, a structural distinction that matters to institutions and advisers assessing sustainability of returns. The release did not disclose an indicative annual percentage yield or detail the specific collateral types the vault currently accepts.

May Wang, co-founder of ValueChain, framed the integration as a diversification of the ecosystem’s opportunity set further along the risk spectrum, consistent with ValueChain’s stated aim of giving self-custodial investors access to a range of on-chain financial products alongside spot and perpetuals trading and AI-powered research.

For Morpho, the deal is primarily a distribution move into Asia-Pacific. Shanshan Shui, APAC go-to-market lead at Morpho, said the integration allows the protocol to reach SoDEX and SoSoValue users inside their existing interface, rather than requiring those users to navigate to Morpho directly.

Market context

The integration illustrates a structural pattern that has accelerated across the DeFi and crypto-adjacent fintech space: protocols such as Morpho, Aave and Compound are increasingly positioned as shared yield infrastructure that product teams embed rather than replicate. Morpho’s publicly listed partners include Coinbase, Robinhood and Société Générale, which signals an appetite among regulated and semi-regulated distribution platforms to access on-chain credit yield without building the underlying credit infrastructure themselves.

From a regulatory standpoint, the product occupies a zone that regulators in multiple jurisdictions are actively examining. In the European Union, the Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation came into full application in 2024 and covers certain stablecoin and crypto-asset service activities, though pure DeFi protocols sit in a grey area pending further Commission guidance. In Singapore, where ValueChain is based, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has indicated that yield-bearing digital-asset products may attract licensing requirements depending on their structure. Neither ValueChain nor Morpho addressed the regulatory framing of the earn product in the release.

Unified Labs’ role as vault curator is the risk-management layer that makes the product viable for a broader audience. Louis Wan, co-founder and chief executive of Unified Labs, said Morpho is becoming the yield layer that fintech platforms integrate rather than rebuild, which captures the infrastructure logic of the arrangement. Whether the vault’s curated parameters are sufficient to satisfy institutional or regulated-platform risk standards will depend on how Unified Labs documents and publishes its collateral and allocation methodology over time.

Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

Cross River Bank’s parent company has agreed to acquire branded-wallet specialist Accrue, the businesses announced Tuesday.

The value of the deal was not disclosed – nor was a timeline: Fort Lee, New Jersey-based Cross River said “the transaction is subject to customary closing conditions.”

Acquiring New York City-based Accrue would bolster Cross River’s customer-loyalty capabilities, letting users earn and track incentives in a way that “offer[s] partners a complete embedded finance stack,” the $8.5 billion-asset bank said.

Accrue’s branded-wallet platform “enables merchants to connect stored value, payments, rewards and customer engagement,” the fintech said. The company launched in 2021 as a save-now, buy-later platform but has shifted its focus over time.

Cross River, for its part, already touts “embedded financial solutions across accounts, cards, payments, lending, digital assets and agentic commerce.”

“Payments and loyalty are becoming one,” Cross River CEO Gilles Gade said Tuesday in a statement. “Every brand wants its own wallet, and with Accrue, all of our clients can now build one on our platform.”

With the acquisition, Accrue CEO Michael Hershfield will “take on a leadership role building out Cross River’s embedded finance offerings.” The Accrue team is also set to join the bank through the transaction.

“I started Accrue with the belief that financial products would increasingly live inside the brands and experiences customers use every day,” Hershfield said in a statement. “Accrue brings that to life by embedding wallets, payments, stored value and rewards directly into the merchant experience. Cross River shares that vision, and with its technology, scale and global reach, we can take it much further.”

title: Butter Payments has been sold
snippet: The company was purchased last month, said its former chief executive, Charles Rosenblatt, who noted intensifying competitive pressures.
fullText:
Butter Payments, a business that has provided services to companies for managing customers’ subscription payments, has been acquired.

The company’s ex-CEO, Charles Rosenblatt, disclosed the sale in an interview last week. “We sold it about three weeks ago,” he said during a Friday interview. On his LinkedIn profile, Rosenblatt said the transaction took place in September.

He declined to name the company that has purchased Butter Payments, but said he expected the acquirer would make an announcement.

Butter Payments' business uses machine-learning algorithms and data from a consumer’s card and payment patterns to better understand why a subscription payment failed and how to resolve the problem. 

“Non-sufficient funds is usually the leading source, but another one of the big ones is suspected fraud,” Rosenblatt said in a February interview.

In a press release earlier this year, Butter Payments cited the churn added up to a collective $440 billion annually in lost revenue for companies with subscription payment methods.

During the interview last week, Rosenblatt explained how the payments business has changed so that services like those offered by Butter Payments have been absorbed into broader suites of services owned by larger companies, causing more competitive pressure from bigger players. It was “very tough as a monoline business,” he said. 

Rosenblatt likened the Butter Payments service to one of the myriad items listed on a restaurant’s menu. “What we built was better than anyone else, but for other companies, we were page 18 of a 20-page Cheesecake Factory menu,” Rosenblatt explained. “We were a better page 18. The problem is, what happens, competitively, is folks come in and offer page 18 for free, if you buy pages one through 17.” 

Digital payments juggernaut Stripe being one of those competitors was part of the problem. Rosenblatt shared how one client told him about the unbeatable offer that Stripe made.

“Stripe basically said to them, all the money they're saving you, we'll just pay you that in cash and take it off your bill to not do business with them and stay with us for everything,” Rosenblatt said. “It's hard to beat that, and that was millions of dollars.”

Facing that kind of competition would have required Butter Payments to raise more funds, so developing an exit plan became the more viable option, the ex-CEO said.

“We had a couple new products, but we … would have had to go raise a ridiculous amount of money to go expand,” Rosenblatt said. “Our investors, candidly, didn't have an appetite for that.”

As of February, the San Francisco-based business had raised nearly $40 million as of earlier this year. At its peak size, Butter Payments had about 53 employees.

Rosenblatt joined Butter Payments in June 2025 as its chief commercial officer, according to his LinkedIn profile. In November of last year, he was promoted to CEO, with marching orders to turn the business around after excessive spending, he said.

Prior to that role, he has been an adviser to investment companies and previously a payments consultant, but he had also held executive posts at companies including PayQuicker, Payoneer and Velo Payments, his LinkedIn profile showed.

Rosenblatt said he has counseled other companies with standalone approaches similar to the Butter Payments business to be aware of the encroaching competition.

“My big message is, I think you're going to have a hard time as a standalone doing this,” Rosenblatt contended.

As for Rosenblatt, he plans to return to the cross-border payments niche where he spent much of his career. He’s on the hunt for new opportunities at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas this week.

The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering.

  

            						

On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.

All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.

In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.

Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.

title: 7X Launches ADEED Finance to Link UAE SME Supply Chains to Banks
snippet: The logistics group's fintech arm FINTX has built a digital referral platform connecting SME financing needs to five UAE banks. The post 7X Launches ADEED Finance to Link UAE SME Supply Chains to Banks appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
7X, the UAE-based trade, transport and logistics group, has launched ADEED Finance, a digital platform designed to channel small and medium-sized enterprise financing applications to a network of participating banks. The platform is built and operated by FINTX, the group’s in-house fintech arm, and sits within the broader ADEED ecosystem that 7X introduced earlier in 2026 as a supply chain support platform for the UAE business environment.

The initial partner network comprises First Abu Dhabi Bank, Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, Emirates NBD, National Bank of Fujairah and Numou. Together they cover a range of financing pathways including trade finance, working capital, supply chain finance, receivables and invoice financing, letters of credit, bank guarantees and Sharia-compliant structures. Each institution retains full independence over credit assessment and lending decisions; ADEED Finance acts as a structured referral and documentation channel rather than a lender in its own right.

The deal

Tariq Al Wahedi, group CEO of 7X, described the logic of connecting logistics infrastructure to financing access: “As logistics, finance and data become increasingly interconnected, the strength of this relationship is shaping the speed, continuity and efficiency of trade.”

Malaz Mubaid, CEO of FINTX, emphasised the platform’s role as neutral infrastructure. “We have developed the platform as scalable digital infrastructure capable of accommodating the different products, requirements and business models of our partners, while preserving each institution’s complete independence in credit assessment and decision-making,” he said.

The platform captures financing requirements in their commercial and operational context, bundling the documentation each institution needs alongside the application. The company says this makes the process more transparent for both businesses and lenders, though it has not published data on application approval rates or average processing times.

Market context

The ADEED Finance model reflects a broader pattern in Gulf fintech: logistics and trade platforms are increasingly adding financial services layers to deepen their value proposition and generate ancillary revenue, rather than relying solely on transactional or operational fees. Comparable approaches have emerged across Southeast Asia, where supply chain platforms have sought to monetise access to trade data by facilitating working capital facilities alongside freight and warehousing services.

In the UAE, the regulatory environment is supportive. The Central Bank of the UAE has published frameworks for digital lending and fintech sandbox participation, and the wider Abu Dhabi Global Market and Dubai International Financial Centre regulatory sandboxes have both encouraged embedded finance and supply chain finance innovation. The ADEED Finance model, as a referral platform rather than a balance-sheet lender, carries a lighter regulatory footprint than a direct lending proposition, which may speed the expansion of its bank partner network.

The SME financing gap in the Gulf remains structurally significant. Access to trade finance is frequently cited in World Trade Organization and International Finance Corporation assessments as a constraint on SME growth in the MENA region, with collateral requirements and documentation complexity as the primary friction points. A structured digital channel that presents applications in their operational context could reduce that friction at the origination stage, though whether it materially improves approval rates will depend on how the participating banks integrate the data into their credit workflows. The platform’s next expansion milestone is the addition of further financial institution partners and financing pathways, which FINTX indicated would continue as the ecosystem matures.

Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026, Guildhall, City of London

Delivered: 20 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Highlights

In an ever-changing environment, our strategy is our anchor. Our priorities – supporting growth, being a smarter regulator, helping consumers and fighting financial crime – help us decide consistently and act for the long term.  

While we are past the peak of rule making, we are still taking a deliberate, strategic approach to reform rather than taking a piecemeal approach.

We encourage firms to engage with us. Tell us where the friction lies so we can build a system that works together.

Look around.

This building has stood for more than 600 years. It’s survived both the Great Fire and the Blitz. 

And yet it still endures. Because when it had to be, it was rebuilt deliberately.

That’s the lesson I want to borrow tonight.

The world around Guildhall looks nothing like it did – and neither does your industry. Technology and AI mean markets are changing faster, and more fundamentally, than ever before.

But one thing is constant. 

Markets have always been rooted in trust.

Trust is fundamental to the success of your sector.

And it is a successful sector. 

London ranks second globally in the Global Financial Centres Index, just behind New York.

And millions trust you with their savings. Their pensions. Their very futures.

Total assets under management have now reached £16.5tn – that’s nearly 5 times the UK’s GDP.

But success is no reason to stand still.  

    

            						

Reform: more than writing rules

In this sector, we’re just past peak rule making.  

The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.

But we’re not done yet.

We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.

Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.

It takes a strategic approach.  

One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions. 

And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.

In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.

We’ve introduced targeted support.

And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.

We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.

So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.

We’re already seeing real progress.

Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.

And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.

These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.

But it’s well worth it.

          

            						

Our report card

Last year we set out a new 5-year strategy.

To support growth, be a smarter regulator, help consumers navigate their financial lives and fight financial crime.

These aren’t separate goals. Each one helps us do our job of making markets work well.  

We’re pleased with the progress we’ve made so far.

Our latest Practitioner Panel survey found that three quarters of firms have high trust in us, and the same proportion support our strategy.

More than 7 in 10 agree our work enhances the UK’s reputation as a financial centre.  

And nearly 9 in 10 now understand the Consumer Duty’s requirements – a big change from last year.

But we know there’s more to do. 

Which is why we’ll stay focused on reducing burden, including by simplifying data returns.

And expand our innovation services, where applications rose 89% in the first year of our strategy.

From our Scale-up Unit to our AI sandboxes, we’re helping firms access funding, test new ideas and innovate more quickly.

And we’ll keep sharing what we learn to help firms innovate effectively. 

          

            						

Challenges ahead

Still, financial crime remains a challenge – at home and abroad.

In the UK, investment fraud losses alone rose 40% in 2025.  

And that’s despite us being ever more assertive.

We’re securing more criminal convictions than ever before across fraud, money laundering and insider dealing.

Last year, we issued over 2,300 scam and unauthorised firm warnings.

And in recent weeks, we’ve made 3 arrests as part of a major insider dealing investigation and helped the Metropolitan Police disrupt a suspected serious organised crime network.

But intervention is just part of the equation.

Regulator and industry alike have to help consumers use financial services safely.

The Investment Association has Savvy the Squirrel to help build confidence to invest.

And we have Emil the Seal to point people to our Firm Checker.

Since its launch in January, consumers have used it nearly 2 million times to make sure firms are authorised and genuine.

A partnership between Emil and Savvy could be a powerful one, especially if firms point consumers to Firm Checker. 

What is clear is that with the speed and scale of this threat, we can’t do this on our own.

This fight calls for a system-wide response – because scams undermine trust, market integrity and consumer confidence.

So work with us.

In July, we published our review of financial crime controls in asset management and alternatives.

We found good practice and room for improvement – particularly in higher-risk areas, such as private markets.

Our message is clear: tailor your financial crime controls to the risks.

Our ask is clear, too: share intelligence early. Flag the gaps in the system. And help us stop criminals exploiting them.

It’s how markets stay trusted and confident.

          

            						

Working differently to support a changing world

Change is happening at a breakneck speed.

More technology. More cross-border activity. More innovation.

All moving faster than traditional regulation can keep up with.  

Which is why we’re not just regulating for the market as it is today. We’re future-proofing it.

By setting clear, outcomes-focused standards, using better data to spot emerging risks and keeping our rules under review as markets evolve.  

That approach keeps us open-minded in the face of change. 

And our regulation and rulebook proportionate and fit for the future.  

Take the package of reforms we consulted on this summer. By streamlining the rulebook for asset managers, we could save firms £128m per year.  

Our proposed fund reporting framework is part of that: simpler reporting for firms, better data for us to consider as we review our rules and see how markets are operating.  

We’re collecting responses until Thursday, so there’s still time to have your say. 

I’ve always said we can’t regulate just for yesterday’s challenges. We have to let markets evolve.  

And we are.

We worked previously to support industry and IA-led blueprints for fund tokenisation.  

Now, we’re helping firms put them into practice.

Baillie Gifford tested the technology behind its tokenised fund in our regulatory sandbox. That fund was authorised in under a year.  

Next month, our joint tokenisation roadmap with the Bank of England will set the path from testing to lasting infrastructure for markets as a whole.  

But change also demands preparation.  

With T+1 settlement less than a year away, we are focused on this sector’s readiness.

So be prepared – because we will act if you’re not. 

After all, market integrity is at stake. 

Getting outcomes-focused regulation right means you don’t need to wait for new rules to innovate.

And this will move us beyond a cycle of constant rule making to one of us checking that our rules work as intended.

We already do this regularly.  

You’ve seen it in the removal of rules requiring a 7-day delay in initial public offerings. 

Our review of the Consumer Duty’s application to wholesale markets. 

And our Advice Guidance Boundary Review and unbundling of research rules.

You’ve also just heard me say we’re just past the peak of rule making.

While it may not feel like it yet, it will eventually – I promise!  

When it does, our focus will be clear. 

Keep what works. Fix what doesn’t. And keep growth and innovation at the centre of it.

          

            						

Becoming the regulator of the future

Being the right kind of regulator means being right for today and tomorrow.

Later this week at Mansion House, our chief executive will speak about what a changing world means for modern regulators.

The same question applies here.

There are more opportunities – for firms and criminals – than ever before. And we have to meet them differently. 

By making better use of data and technology and focusing our supervision where risk actually sits.

AI already helps us cut through large data sets to identify risks sooner and act more quickly.

We'll keep exploring where we can go from here. Because we don’t know what tomorrow holds.

But we know we have to be a regulator that moves as fast as the market does, without losing the judgement that makes us worth trusting.

And you have to be an industry that’s just as intentional. One that moves quickly where it counts, without losing sight of the people who depend on you.

          

            						

A shared responsibility

We all want a more predictable, proportionate and purposeful regulatory system.

We’ll only get there by being deliberate, with the future in mind – as this building reminds us.

So, keep telling us where the tension is, and continue engaging with the reforms already underway.

The prize is worth it: a regulatory framework that supports growth and encourages investment while protecting consumers and earning trust.

Not just for today – but for tomorrow.

title: Shopping is Muse’s top task: Meta
snippet: About a quarter of the personal agent’s earliest adopters look to shop, with an average purchase size around $200, Meta’s CEO said.
fullText:
Dive Brief:

Shopping is the most common activity for Meta Platforms’ new Muse personal artificial intelligence agent, with an average purchase size of $200, CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Wednesday during a conference call to report quarterly income. About 25% of Muse users task it with shopping, including travel planning, he said. Digital payments processor Stripe handles some payments.

In the first week of the Muse agent’s release last month, Meta “had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits, since the volumes were above what any of us expected,” Zuckerberg said, without offering any specifics about agentic transactions or payments. About 10 million people have signed up for a Muse agent, in the U.S. and Canada, the initial two markets, he said. Meta uses Stripe’s Link digital wallet as the Muse payment method.

Beyond agentic shopping, users’ directions to increase their “personal productivity” and connecting Muse to email and calendars are the next most widely used tasks for the service, Zuckerberg said.

Dive Insight:

Meta’s third-quarter earnings report Wednesday was its first since the Sept. 8 debut of the personal AI agent. Meta describes the digital agent as one that requires no technical experience and “no learning curve.”

Stripe charted a significant increase in agentic commerce, starting last month, the company’s president, John Collison, said last week, during a podcast he hosts. He described the increase in the bot-driven commerce as he conversed with Zuckerberg, saying the Stripe agentic activity “started going vertical,” in September. Collison’s brother Patrick Collison, who is Stripe’s CEO, sits on Meta’s board of directors.

Muse, along with personal agents like Instinct, and the open source agent OpenClaw, are viewed by some in the payments industry as the likeliest gateways for agentic commerce to expand into agent-driven consumer transactions.

The topic of AI-driven commerce – including agentic transactions and whether a “human in the loop” model will ever yield to fully machine-driven payments – was a major topic of discussion at the annual Money20/20 financial technology conference this week in Las Vegas.

Agentic spending remains far from ready for mass public use, with multiple parties in the retail ecosystem still needing to sort out a variety of issues, including liability, Early Warning Services CEO Cameron Fowler said Monday in an interview. 

EWS is a consortium owned by seven of the largest U.S. banks, several of which have moved to block access by AI agents such as Muse to their customers’ accounts. JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank, was among the first to do so, with CEO Jamie Dimon discussing the issue last week on the company’s quarterly earnings call.

“Turning that engine onto spending our money for us is just such a wildly different proposition, and almost none of the customer protections that you would expect to see are in place,” said Fowler, a former banking executive with Montreal-based BMO Financial Group.

Muse is available only in the U.S. and Canada as costs for the computing infrastructure powering the service remain too cost-prohibitive for a wider global release, Zuckerberg said.

“If we actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that (user) number to be significantly larger than what we're seeing today,” he said. “But then on the flip side, we actually have to go do the work to bring the efficiency in line to make that make sense, and so that's a big part of it that we need to do.”

Meta will work to make money from Muse sooner than its “normal playbook” for products, Zuckerberg said, owing to the operating costs of computing infrastructure and the size of the opportunity the company sees for personal agents.

Meta aims to connect Muse agents with billions of people and evolve it into a broader Muse network that includes businesses interacting with their own agents, the billionaire founder and CEO said. Meta is the parent company of social media sites Instagram and Facebook.
