fullText:
Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House.

  

Speaker: Nikhil Rathi, chief executive 

Event: Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner 

Delivered: 22 October 2026 

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Highlights

The UK’s financial services strength provides a platform to lead the next era of technology-driven growth. 

We must move faster and focus on outcomes to protect market integrity without holding back innovation. 

The FCA will make better use of technology and intelligence and more assertive use of its powers to tackle system-wide risks and financial crime. 

Stronger partnerships between regulators, industry, government and others is essential to protect market integrity.

    

            						

The success of the UK’s financial services

In August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston.   

A Red Sox game, perhaps? No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.

Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life. Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.

Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.

It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.

On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters. Yet there’s plenty to cheer.

We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…

A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of…  

Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.

UK firms leading in:

artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.

consumer access to investment opportunities widened.

moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.

Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City. Thank you for your leadership.

If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

          

            						

I say 'we' because the FCA plays an important role.

Financial services businesses and investors need confidence in markets…including their ability to withstand and recover from shocks.

That’s why ensuring the integrity of the financial services system is an FCA primary objective.

Tonight, I want to explain how we maintain it as technology accelerates exponentially. Because, while we may be getting past peak rule making, we are nowhere near peak reform or innovation. Nor past the peak intervention required to disrupt harm and support market integrity and growth.

We have seen radical technological change before… But never so widespread or disruptive. Nor combined, as now, with a new geopolitical and defence order.

The trouble is our system responds too slowly. And trust in institutions is eroded if we can’t solve problems quickly.

Regulation takes time. Legislation requires scrutiny. Parliamentary resource is precious.

Our judicial system is under immense pressure, with more litigation and weightier decisions. We risk delays becoming the norm, with legal claims written with AI’s help potentially making things worse.

We all play a part in a system that prioritises safety in process over ruthless focus on outcomes and delivery.

So, the UK finds itself in a dangerous 'innovation delta': where institutions tasked with regulating markets and the mechanisms holding us accountable lag behind.

If we maintain an analogue approach in a digital age, new products enter the market faster than we adapt… Leaving us reacting to, even overwhelmed by, changes rather than shaping conditions for the UK to thrive.

Take Meta Muse, launched 6 weeks ago, one of the fastest-downloaded apps in US history. Personal agents are profoundly changing how consumers interact with financial and health services. Such applications will reach UK consumers soon.

Frontier AI models are here, making it easier for AI agents to carry out tasks increasingly autonomously. You are fast adopters.

And rapid change in wholesale markets:

decentralised finance

24/7 trading a reality with prices increasingly forming over weekends

parallel market structures operating alongside traditional ones

Vast opportunities. But the threats to market integrity are as serious as I have seen them.

Unprecedented volatility, concentration risks, new forms of market abuse and rampant cross-border financial crime: fast-emerging technologies putting these on steroids.

Cyber security too mixes the frailties of human nature and high tech.

Our own AI minister recently said it was likely that at some point the UK’s systems will be breached. Which is why reporting and learning from near misses is so important. As is insurance for you, your customers and supply chain.

Prevention will not always work, so investment in recovery is a necessity. The gravity of the decision to press a kill switch may pale in significance with the enormity of the task to get a system running again.

In the face of all today’s challenges, the temptation is to say: 'write more rules, but do it damned well faster'.

We will, where we need to… Including aligning with any national or global AI standards, which the Prime Minister has said will be a focus of the UK’s upcoming G20 presidency.

But if policymaking is our only regulatory reflex, we’ll be stuck chasing yesterday’s market instead of embracing the one in front of us.

          

            						

Regulatory reform continues

I do not mean to suggest that we will slow down rule reform or modernisation. But our focus must be on outcomes.

We have reformed our rulebook and strengthened our operations. Capital market reforms have kicked in. 

Technology is making it easier to interact with us with reduced reporting burdens. Our widest ever range of innovation services with record demand.

And we promised less intensive supervision for those clearly trying to do the right thing, so we can focus where harm is greatest.

But the impact won’t be fully felt unless we also end tickbox compliance. Reams of potentially duplicative assurance – data packs, risk reports, internal audit. Some of these processes driven by commercial choice, others by regulation and legislation.

Sarah Pritchard, the FCA’s deputy chief executive, will engage with you to streamline unnecessary effort…. To give Boards confidence to be brave. And consider if it’s time to look again at the 3 lines of defence.

As much as 8% of banks’ workforces are dedicated to combatting crime. We should be delivering far better outcomes with those resources.

Yet we’re bogged down by excessive data collection, complex validation, and a limited ability to understand a customer’s wider context and identify risks that span borders, institutions and accounts…

As we integrate over 60,000 professional services businesses into our ambit, Johan Sekora, our new chief operating officer, who previously led Swedish banks' intelligence sharing efforts, will spearhead work to look beyond know your customer (KYC) process so we unearth actual money laundering.

Information collected through KYC, transaction and sanctions monitoring will remain valuable.

We are ready to experiment, so we can focus collective resources exactly where they are needed….

Within the FCA, too, we must continue to get better at joining up the dots. AI tools give our supervisors a richer risk picture…

…Agents can assess cases, synthesise returns and intelligence… parse millions of rows of data and identify missing or concerning information…

Freeing up our people to do the work we need experts to do: to make the hardest decisions… Such as when agentic coordination becomes market manipulation. Or judging when a risk becomes system-wide.

Expanded capability means we’ll find more risks. So, we’ll need to be open about which justify the use of resources and which don’t.

          

            						

Powers and partnership

As an institution, we have not always persuaded others of the need for legislative change… And even when we have, change has been welcome but often slow.

So: how can we do our job effectively when technology advances faster than we can write laws or rules?

The answer must be to rethink how we use powers we already have.

We have system-wide responsibilities, but a fixed view of who we explicitly regulate.

Government and Parliament decide who we authorise. This perimeter is our anchor. But we cannot let it weigh so heavily that it sinks the regulatory ship.

Today’s risks aren’t polite enough to knock on our door to introduce themselves.

Market, cyber, or criminal risks emerge from multiple networks, firms and jurisdictions….

Capital flows across sectors, regulated or not, creating complex webs of commercial incentives. And harms within our remit originating outside it. Be that mass digital harm on social media.

Insider trading on offshore gambling or prediction markets. Or outages – like Google Cloud this week – disrupting people’s access to vital services. Talk of such system-wide risks is far from academic.

Money laundering through the regulated system is not just about fraud, sanctions and tax evasion, it funds human and drugs trafficking. Their victims: society’s most vulnerable.

Parliament has provided tools to deal with such system-wide issues affecting our objectives and remit:

The Enterprise, Consumer Rights and Online Safety and Digital Market Acts to name 4.

The critical third-parties regime. An expanding anti-money-laundering remit.

It isn’t enough to ask: is this in our perimeter?

If significant harm affects markets within our remit, we should ask: what powers do we have to tackle it? Would this be a good use of resources?

The same is true of growth opportunities. Not what are they, but how can we enable them?

In every instance: who can we work with to make a difference, quickly? Because no single agency can rise to today’s challenges alone.

Working with the Met, National Crime Agency and HMRC, we’ve recently undertaken 2 of our most significant operations to disrupt suspected organised criminal gangs who seek to abuse our financial system.

So, effective partnerships are already in action:

Cooperation through the Digital Regulators Forum on Meta Muse.

A big delivery year for pensions with the Pensions Regulator and DWP.

A FCA-Bank of England roadmap on digital assets soon dovetailing with the work Chris Woolard and the industry have been doing.

And work with international counterparts.

Recent action by US authorities against anti-money laundering violations confirming the fight against financial crime remains global. 

          

            						

Call to action: we need you

We should also be open to ideas about how we can act at pace and scale.

We have seen dedicated financial services courts speed things up in other markets, for example… And the accountability system could foster collaborative working.

There are significant mechanisms to hold the FCA accountable, more than for most regulators. Appropriate given the significance of our work and the breadth of powers entrusted to us.

But accountability must be system-wide too. Whether that is to press hard on growth or engage on risks, and which are priorities and which aren’t.

Parliament is the only body that can ensure accountability across rather than within narrow remits, transcending traditional committee boundaries.

And as we significantly step up the intensity of our activity to address system-wide risks, we need you.

The earlier we can work with you – the firms we regulate and civil society – to identify emerging risks and opportunities, the faster we can give you the confidence to move.

          

            						

Close: the prize

In other words, partnership.

That is what we need now. Partnership not just between financial regulators but more widely.

Only through partnership can we deliver the system-wide response needed to protect market integrity. And that is the foundation necessary so innovation can flourish, productivity can rise and growth can endure.

The UK is incredibly well placed to harness the power of new technology. The existing strength of this sector gives us a genuine head start.

If we can harness technological progress – if we continue to lead – financial services can place the UK at the forefront of this new era of innovation.

As regulators, we are committed to creating the conditions for you to do that.

Together, we can build a future that the whole country will be proud of…

title: Xsolla Adds Co-Marketing Tool Linking Payment Providers to Game Devs
snippet: Xsolla's self-serve Co-Marketing Campaigns tool lets payment providers run cashback and promotional deals directly with video game developers. The post Xsolla Adds Co-Marketing Tool Linking Payment Providers to Game Devs appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Xsolla, the Los Angeles-based gaming commerce company, has unveiled Co-Marketing Campaigns, a self-serve feature within its Business Account for Payment Providers platform. The tool lets payment providers initiate, manage and launch promotional campaigns, such as cashback offers, directly with video game developers, without requiring a separate workflow or intermediary negotiation. 

The product addresses a gap that Xsolla has identified in the gaming payments value chain. Payment providers process substantial transaction volumes across video games but have historically had little visibility into how their methods perform by title or developer, and no standardised route to translate that data into marketing partnerships. The new tool is designed to close both gaps inside a single dashboard.

How the workflow operates

Chris Hewish, president of Xsolla

The four-step process runs entirely within the provider’s existing Xsolla Business Account. Providers first review analytics showing which games generate the strongest uptake for their payment method. They then configure a campaign, selecting parameters such as a cashback percentage linked to a specific title. The request is sent to the relevant developer, who must accept before anything goes live. Once both parties have agreed, Xsolla handles the technical setup and the promotion appears at checkout inside Xsolla Pay Station and on a dedicated landing page.

Chris Hewish, president of Xsolla, framed the commercial logic clearly: “Payment providers have long competed mostly on rate. Co-Marketing Campaigns give them a way to win on more than that, with promotions built around the video games their customers already play. It turns a payment relationship into a marketing one, and it runs from the account they already have.”

Xsolla also noted it is developing additional initiatives for banks and financial institutions, including loyalty point integrations, branded in-game stores and cardholder promotions tied to gaming audiences. No timeline or named partners were provided for these broader banking initiatives.

Market context

The gaming payments sector is a significant but structurally underserved vertical. Xsolla claims reach across more than 1,500 game developers and operates as merchant of record in more than 200 geographies, with access to over 1,000 local payment methods. That network density is the commercial foundation on which Co-Marketing Campaigns depends: the tool has limited value without a large enough catalogue of games for providers to select from and a sizable enough player base to make promotional economics work.

The broader competitive dynamic is relevant here. Payment providers in gaming have typically differentiated on acceptance rates, local method coverage and settlement speed. Adding a marketing dimension shifts the competitive frame. If Xsolla can demonstrate measurable lift in payment method preference from cashback campaigns, it repositions the platform from a processing intermediary to a performance marketing channel for providers, a more defensible and higher-margin role.

For payment providers, the question will be whether the campaign economics justify the effort. Cashback promotions in gaming tend to work well with younger, price-sensitive audiences, but they require careful yield management. The self-serve framing suggests Xsolla is aiming for scale across many smaller campaigns rather than a small number of bespoke deals, which is the right structural bet if the developer network is deep enough to support it.

The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). There was a 27-percentage point increase in firms’ understanding of the Secondary International Competitiveness and Growth Objective and a 25-percentage point increase in confidence in our delivery of it.

We took on board feedback from last year’s survey and provided further guidance to help firms embed the Consumer Duty. This year, 88% of firms say they understand what we expect on supporting consumers and embedding the Duty.

The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'

Matt Hammerstein, chair of the FCA Practitioner Panel, said: 'This year’s survey results indicate firms continue to have broadly positive views of the FCA, including strong understanding of expectations under the Consumer Duty and significant growth in confidence in the FCA’s ability to deliver on its secondary objectives focused on growth and competitiveness.

'The Panel is encouraging the FCA to be clearer about the outcomes it expects its priorities to produce, and more vocal about the progress it is making against these, to strengthen confidence in the UK as a leading global financial centre and attractive place to invest.'

In the first year of our strategy, we've delivered an estimated £5.6bn in benefits to consumers and the economy, including launching My FCA, reducing reporting burdens to save firms around £16m annually, and introducing nearly 50 pro-growth measures to boost UK competitiveness and innovation. 

Since the survey was conducted, we’ve continued our work to deliver landmark reforms, including working with HM Treasury and the Financial Ombudsman Service to modernise the redress framework, support industry delivery of the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, regulating Buy Now Pay Later products, establishing a new regime for cryptoassets, and progressing the PISCES private markets framework.

title: LendWell Signs Multi-Year AI Mortgage Deal with SPF Private Clients
snippet: The Irish AI mortgage platform will deploy across SPF's UK mortgage and protection workflows, with a broader rollout planned for 2027. The post LendWell Signs Multi-Year AI Mortgage Deal with SPF Private Clients appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
LendWell, an Irish AI-native mortgage origination platform, has signed a multi-year agreement with SPF Private Clients, one of the UK’s larger independent mortgage and protection intermediaries. Implementation is already underway, with a full rollout scheduled for 2027. The company describes the deal as its most significant UK partnership to date.

SPF Private Clients, which employs more than 200 people and has been part of the Howden Group since 2022, will use LendWell’s platform across mortgage and protection case workflows. The technology is designed to handle document preparation, case follow-up and administrative coordination, using the context already present in a case to carry out defined tasks for adviser review. Professional responsibility for advice remains with SPF’s advisers; LendWell’s scope is the operational and administrative layer around those decisions.

What LendWell actually does

Jamie Lawless, co-founder and CEO at LendWell

The platform’s commercial proposition targets a well-documented structural problem in mortgage broking: a substantial share of skilled adviser time is consumed by administration rather than client-facing work. LendWell extracts information from documents, calls and communications, links it to supporting evidence, and surfaces it within the case workflow for adviser sign-off. The aim is to increase throughput without a proportional increase in headcount.

James Rodea, managing director at SPF Private Clients

Jamie Lawless, co-founder and chief executive of LendWell, said: “Mortgage technology has spent years digitising processes, but digitising manual work isn’t the same as removing it. Too much mortgage expertise is still consumed by administration. The aim isn’t to replace professional judgement, it’s to make better use of it.”

James Rodea, managing director at SPF Private Clients, said the firm was drawn to LendWell’s focus on reducing the work around advice while integrating with its existing systems, giving it flexibility to introduce the technology on its own terms.

Market context and regulatory considerations

The SPF agreement follows LendWell’s earlier deployment with Finance Solutions, the mortgage broking arm of Howden Ireland, described as Ireland’s largest mortgage broker. That live deployment gives LendWell a reference case in a regulated environment, which matters when selling into large UK intermediaries where risk appetite around new technology is directly shaped by FCA expectations on operational resilience and consumer outcomes under the Consumer Duty framework.

LendWell enters a UK mortgage technology market that has attracted meaningful investment, with platforms competing across origination, sourcing and post-sale servicing. The differentiated pitch here is AI applied to the case workflow itself rather than front-end comparison or lender connectivity. Several UK-based and US-originated mortgage workflow tools are pursuing adjacent ground, though the regulated intermediary segment remains less saturated than the direct-to-consumer channel.

The FCA’s Consumer Duty, which came into full effect in 2023 and extended to closed products in 2024, places a higher bar on intermediaries to demonstrate that advice processes serve client outcomes rather than operational convenience. AI tooling that demonstrably increases adviser capacity for client-facing work is broadly consistent with that regulatory direction, provided the audit trail for case decisions is clear and responsibility for advice remains unambiguously with the adviser. LendWell’s stated architecture, where AI prepares and coordinates while the adviser reviews and approves, is designed with that line in mind.

The next milestones to watch are the pace of the 2027 SPF rollout, any further UK intermediary signings, and whether LendWell moves toward FCA authorisation in its own right or continues to operate as a technology supplier within its clients’ regulated frameworks.

fullText:
Speech by Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges, at the Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026.

  

Speaker: Jon Relleen, director of infrastructure and exchanges 

Event: Reform of the UK Public and Private Capital Markets Summit 2026

Delivered: 5 October 2026  

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 9 minutes

Highlights:

The FCA’s wide-ranging reforms over recent years are making UK capital markets more effective, competitive and attractive.

Trust, market integrity and high standards set the foundations for sustainable growth, and it is crucial that we also enable informed risk-taking.

We’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets by supporting innovation, including tokenisation.

    

            						

The Economic Secretary to the Treasury has discussed the contribution of UK markets to economic growth. 

I want to build on that by talking about the FCA’s role in reforming capital market rules.

The headline is that we've been very busy over the past few years. 

We’ve now completed major aspects of a multi-year programme of work, to ensure capital markets work well for our economy and support growth.

This has already delivered positive changes. But there’s plenty more to come.

We are working on further reforms, while also adapting to rapid changes in markets and use of technology.

In fact, areas such as tokenisation, AI and markets for trading private company shares have become central to our capital markets policy programme. 

And that tells us something important. As markets change, our approach has had to change too.

The question has not been whether regulation changes. It has been how we adjust in a way that preserves trust while also supporting innovation and growth.

Let me start by talking about our approach to the work.

We have been working with the Treasury, the Bank of England and in close dialogue with the private sector, on a raft of wholesale market reforms.

These draw on formal reports, like the Wholesale Markets Review, our process of reviewing inherited EU regulation, and issues raised by market contacts.

Some have suggested the work programme is a list not a strategy. But I think that underestimates it. There are some key principles running through it.

          

            						

Reforming from a position of strength

First, we are reforming from a position of strength, by building on the UK’s advantages.

The UK is home to deep, trusted and internationally connected capital markets. 

London continues to rank among the world’s leading financial centres. Our markets are respected and characterised by strong institutions and a reputation for integrity.

And the UK offers a full range of markets and services, supported by a diverse system of issuers, investors, intermediaries and infrastructure.

So our work programme is broad too. Covering primary markets, secondary markets, post-trade arrangements and a broad range of assets.

But successful markets cannot stand still.

Capital is increasingly mobile. Technology is reshaping markets. Private markets have grown. And new forms of trading and market infrastructure are emerging.

So our challenge is to preserve these strengths, whilst keeping UK markets dynamic and internationally competitive.

          

            						

Rebalancing risk

In some areas this requires us to think differently about regulation.

For a while, financial regulation became more detailed and prescriptive. Often for understandable reasons following periods of market stress.

But we know that growth, innovation and investment all depend on taking risk.

That is why our approach is founded on the principle of maintaining high standards while creating more space for informed risk-taking and innovation. 

This is especially relevant in wholesale markets, where professional participants assess opportunities and weigh risks every day.

Our role is to create regulation that enables this through clear rules and good disclosures, so that firms and investors can make informed decisions.

This is what we mean when we talk about rebalancing risk.

It does not mean lowering standards or weakening market integrity.

It means being deliberate about where regulation is needed and where market participants can take decisions themselves, armed with good information and appropriate disclosures.

In many cases, that means we can shift away from detailed prescription towards outcomes, transparency and accountability.

In doing so, we must never forget the underlying objective.

Ultimately, we want companies to have good options for how to raise capital, so they can invest and grow. And investors to have access to a broad range of investment opportunities.

Regulation cannot, on its own, drive economic growth. But good regulation and markets that work well are vital for a healthy economy.

          

            						

Turning reform into results

You can see our approach in the reforms we have already delivered.

We have completed around 30 capital-markets focused workstreams. And there’s an even larger number across the FCA’s broader work.

That’s too many to discuss individually in this speech. There’s a list below, but to summarise some of them:

In primary markets, we introduced once-in-a-generation changes to the UK listing regime, significantly reducing costs for issuers and supporting competitiveness with other jurisdictions. Since then, we have seen many corporate transactions that have been simplified as a result. And around 25 companies have joined the Main Market, including 7 IPOs in H1 2026.

Our new public offers framework raised the thresholds for when prospectuses are needed by companies raising capital and we also introduced public offer platforms to facilitate off-market fundraising. We have already seen a rise in capital raised by companies, including via debt markets, alongside the broader benefits of a simpler and more flexible regime.

In secondary markets, we have significantly improved transparency in bond and derivatives markets. This includes the bond consolidated tape, which launched in June – the first consolidated tape outside North America – which already has 1.6 million licences subscribed to it. These changes are shining a new light on UK markets, delivering a 70% increase in corporate bond trades and 30% for government bond trades observed in real time and enhancing the way market participants view the market.

We are moving towards an equity consolidated tape too and will appoint a provider next year. In the meantime, we launched a market activity report, so investors see the true scale of UK equity trading.

We have also responded to the growth of private markets through the creation of PISCES, a new market for trading in private company shares. Four operators have been authorised and we’ve seen seven transactions – involving companies ranging from tech firms, to brewers and board-game makers.

In post-trade, we’ve adjusted transaction reporting, with initial proposals estimated to save firms £100m per year.

And we’ve altered some of the clearing and margining rules, including increasing the clearing threshold for commodity derivatives following volatility in commodity markets.

On the investor side, we are streamlining regulatory requirements for the asset management sector, via the AIFMD review, and supporting the government in its review of the pension market.

We’re also supporting retail participation by improving access to investment advice and simplifying product information.

And our changes to primary market rules have positively impacted retail investment. We’ve seen a 50% increase in the value of retail-denominated corporate bonds and an increase in domestic retail investor allocation in fundraisings.

We are not done though.

A range of further reforms are planned or underway.

For example, on securitisation markets; listed company disclosures; benchmarks; and rules on clearing and margining.

We’re always in listening mode. So if you have ideas that would benefit UK markets please tell us.

          

            						

Competitiveness without compromise

We are doing this work to make markets work better, which is our statutory objective.

By doing that, we support growth and international competitiveness.

Capital is mobile. Businesses have choices about where they raise finance, invest and operate. The UK cannot ignore that reality.

But competitiveness does not come from a race to the bottom.

The UK's reputation for openness, stability and high standards is a strategic asset.

Our approach is pragmatic. We will challenge inherited rules when they no longer serve markets effectively, learn from other jurisdictions, and recognise the value of international consistency.

But we will do so without compromising market integrity, which provides the bedrock for sustainable growth.

          

            						

Preparing for tomorrow’s markets

I want to finish by talking about how we’re preparing for tomorrow’s markets.

We want to support innovation. To ensure markets evolve and use technology that opens up opportunities, efficiencies and encourages new entrants.

One example is working with firms to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI. Through our AI Lab, the AI Consortium with the Bank, and innovation sandboxes that allow firms to test ideas with us. 

And we are enabling firms and markets to explore tokenisation.

With the Bank and Treasury, we set up the Digital Securities Sandbox, which will support issuance of the new digital gilt (or DIGIT) early next year. Many think that the success of DIGIT can catalyse digital activity in UK.

We have worked with industry on new rules and governance for tokenised investment funds and the launch of the UK’s first fully-native tokenised fund.

And with Treasury and the Bank we’ve developed a regulatory framework for stablecoins.

But we are at a critical point. Keeping pace with other jurisdictions will require effective coordination between the private and public sectors. Industry leadership will be at least as important as public policy. 

Firms need to build, scale and innovate, moving beyond pilots to demonstrate real commercial use.

The UK’s Wholesale Digital Markets Champion, Chris Woolard, is playing a key role in coordinating the sector.

We know that regulatory clarity matters too. That’s why in May we published a joint vision with the Bank of England, setting out the regulatory principles for tokenised wholesale markets.

The feedback was clear. Industry wants to move quickly. In turn, we will provide certainty in areas such as prudential treatment, custody and market infrastructure.

We share the sense of urgency.

In coming weeks we will publish a joint roadmap, setting out how the UK’s wholesale markets will adapt as we work collectively to realise the benefits from tokenisation and digitalization.

Our objective is not to predict exactly what future markets will look like.

It is to ensure that our regulatory framework can adapt as markets evolve.

          

            						

Conclusion

We want UK capital markets to remain among the most trusted in the world, whilst also being among the most innovative, competitive and attractive. Markets that allow businesses to raise capital, help investors, and support the wider economy.

Our wide-ranging reforms have already delivered positive outcomes, across a variety of markets.

The approach is to build on the UK’s strengths and enable informed risk-taking, while preserving the trust, integrity and high standards on which successful markets depend.

The programme of reform will continue to evolve as markets change.

But the direction is clear. We are building markets that are ready not only for today's economy but for tomorrow's as well.

          

        

Capital market reforms completed in recent years

The department flagged the potentially fraudulent activity as it seeks to stop criminals from stealing student financial aid payments.

        

            

        Published Oct. 22, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                The Treasury Department has increased its focus on thwarting student financial aid fraud.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

The Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network said this week that it has identified $270 million “in suspicious financial activity” potentially tied to fraud in federal student financial aid programs. It has referred its findings to law enforcement for further investigation, according to a Monday press release.

Since a July alert issued by FinCEN regarding such financial aid fraud, financial institutions have filed about 100 suspicious payment activity reports that led to the agency’s review of some 20,000 suspicious transactions since February, according to Treasury’s release. It noted that such reports are not a complete picture of what may, or may not, be fraud.

“The Trump Administration will not tolerate criminals who exploit government programs for personal gain,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the release. “Treasury is working with financial institutions and law enforcement to identify these fraud schemes, recover stolen funds, and hold those responsible accountable.”

Dive Insight:

Lost taxpayer funds aren’t the only negative impact of financial aid fraud, as it also results in students being deprived of education funds and may saddle some students with debt that is not theirs. It also can result in students not getting into classes with seats taken by fake enrollees.

The increased scrutiny from the government can also slow the processing of legitimate student financial aid applications, Indiana Wesleyan University noted in an August website post.

The July FinCEN alert warned “that schools or their payment contractors often send aid refunds by electronic bank transfer and that the payment description often includes the word ‘refund’ along with the school’s name or initials.” 

The stolen money may travel through payments made by money mules, fake accounts or shell companies that hide the identities of criminals shifting around funds. 

The Treasury release explained how the student aid fraud takes place: Criminals steal personal information – such as names and Social Security numbers – and use them to create fake “ghost students” who are enrolled in classes under an unknowing victim’s identity. Artificial intelligence is making the problem worse.

“Fraudsters may also use super intelligence to produce fake documents that blend stolen information with invented details, which creates what are known as synthetic identities that can pass identity checks,” the release said.

In another type of fraudulent scheme, criminals pay real people for their information so they can create “straw students” to enroll students at schools and take the financial funds that are issued in those names. In some cases, corrupt school employees have helped recruit students and alter records to support the criminal rings, Treasury said.

In keeping with the Trump administration’s crackdown on fraud, Treasury said it’s seeking to further thwart financial aid fraud by increasing cooperation across the federal government and encouraging whistleblowers to come forward with information. In December, the Education Department also noted an increased focus on halting such fraud on its website.

The buy now, pay later provider wants a U.S. charter from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency amid new state rules.

                Sezzle, the buy now, pay later provider, said it has applied with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency to operate a national bank.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Buy now, pay later company Sezzle has applied for a national trust bank charter with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, the company said Thursday in a press release.

If the OCC approves the request, Sezzle’s new bank would offer “a broad range of banking products and services,” including checking and savings accounts, Sezzle said in the release. The company said it aims to target the bank towards “digitally native consumers” who eschew traditional credit products.

“Applying for a national bank charter reflects our commitment to operating under the highest standards of federal oversight,” Sezzle Chief Executive Charlie Youakim said in the press release. If granted, the charter would let Sezzle “offer a broader set of banking products to people who prefer BNPL and digitally native banking products,” under federal supervision, he added.

Dive Insight:

Under the Trump administration, multiple financial technology companies have rushed to apply for OCC charters this year. Block, Ramp, Avant and Modern Treasury are among the fintechs that have sought OCC charters in recent months; Ramp applied last week. 

The national bank charter application represents a pivot from Sezzle’s initial plan to seek a license from Utah regulators to become an industrial loan company.

New BNPL regulations in states such as New York, Illinois and Oregon – along with criticisms from banks and consumer groups about the ILC structure – prompted Sezzle’s change of course from its earlier plan for the Utah license, Youakim said in an August interview. 

The review process by the OCC, the Federal Reserve and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. is expected to take 12 to 18 months, Youakim said.

Minneapolis-based Sezzle has established a niche business among younger and low-income consumers with thin, or zero, credit histories, TD Cowen analyst Hoang Nguyen said in an August interview. 

Nguyen called Sezzle’s decision to seek the OCC charter instead of the state-level ILC “a smart move” given state regulators’ focus on the industry and the potential for tighter lending rules after the Trump administration.

Earlier this year, BNPL rival Affirm Holdings applied in Nevada to operate a bank as an industrial loan company. PayPal Holdings sought a similar license from Utah’s Department of Financial Institutions in December 2025.

title: Fiserv taps AI for retail rethink
snippet: Merchants are grappling with how their payments technology will handle artificial intelligence-fueled digital commerce, a Fiserv executive said.
fullText:
LAS VEGAS – Agentic commerce is forcing digital merchants to assess whether their technology infrastructure is suited to the coming era of shopping agents powered by artificial intelligence, a Fiserv executive said Tuesday. 

Payments involving AI agents introduce new variables into legacy systems that sellers are now considering, Adit Gadgil, Fiserv’s head of global e-commerce and technology for merchant services, said in an interview at a financial technology conference.

“People are trying to fundamentally evaluate: will their legacy payment stack or commerce stack be fit for purpose, or do they need to build a separate, standalone payment stack to solve the needs of the future, which includes stablecoins, which includes agentic traffic?” Gadgil said.

He spoke a day after Fiserv CEO Tsakis Georgakopoulos told an audience Monday at the conference that AI represents “a general-purpose technology because it impacts every part of the value chain and every industry and every business.”

“It is pretty unique compared to everything else we've seen, at least in our lives,” the CEO added during a Monday panel discussion at the Money20/20 financial technology conference with Rodrigo Kede Lima, president of Microsoft Frontier, the software giant’s AI transformation business. “That creates both problems and opportunities for every industry and every customer segment.”

Earlier this year, Milwaukee-based Fiserv announced “a strategic collaboration” with Microsoft to embed AI solutions into Fiserv’s platforms. Fiserv also uses Microsoft’s AI tools for productivity gains among employees.

Consumers have taken to AI chat tools for product discovery, Georgakopoulos noted, “but the complexity is the last mile.”

“Discovery is great,” he said. “How do you actually click that last button, the checkout button, and will that ever become agentic?”

Gadgil said that, as part of the transition to agentic commerce, merchants will also need to accommodate new “machine readable” digital markets where agents will interact with each other – a change that could render some parts of current systems irrelevant.

“Whether we'll be in this situation, where the (online) surface matters so much, is debatable,” Gadgil said. “That doesn't mean it’s going to disappear, but maybe a percentage of it is going to become irrelevant.”

He added that these new “surfaces” will become “a marketplace for agents to work with each other. If you do not have your market agents showing up at these marketplaces, you may not have the opportunity to do business,” Gadgil said.

Agentic payments may drive between $3 trillion and $5 trillion in global consumer commerce by 2030, according to the consulting firm McKinsey.  

In terms of current technology addressing agentic traffic, online sellers haven’t yet experienced a fundamental change in how their businesses operate because most agentic commerce still involves humans permitting transactions after the agent finds products.

“My opinion on this is that agentic today is essentially another channel,” Gadgil said. “From a payment stack perspective, as long as there's a human in the loop on the authorization, actually you don't really need to change that much” after ensuring where the traffic is from and that no fraud is involved.

Larger changes lie farther in the future, when agents begin transacting autonomously, under rules specified by humans.

This shift will involve adding extra steps within the payments flow, to generate at least two receipts to verify an agent’s actions, he said. The first will be at the intent layer, to prove someone authorized the agent to undertake a specific transaction, with the second detailing all the information about the payment.

Fiserv is working to ensure its merchant clients understand these different aspects of verifying consumer intent and the payment level within agentic commerce, Gadgil said.

“They should be careful with the risk they're taking, and it's not just on the merchant side,” he said, noting that issuers, acquirers and card networks will also require detailed data about agentic transactions. 

“Whether it’s the network or the issuer, they’re all going to be asking these questions, asking for more information, because at the end of the day, no one wants to be sitting there with the liability that comes with it,” Gadgil said.

title: Visa changes fees in Canada

fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

A Canadian trade group has urged card networks to reduce their interchange fees and pass those cost savings on to sellers.

        

            

        Published Oct. 21, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Canadian and American flags fly at the Lewiston-Queenston border crossing bridge. San Francisco-based Visa is shifting gears on card fees for merchants in the neighboring country.
            
        
            Joe Raedle via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Starting Oct. 24, Canadian small businesses will pay lower interchange fees to accept Visa credit card payments, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business said in a press release on Wednesday. Visa is cutting interchange fees for companies generating up to CA$750,000 ($534,000) in annual Visa sales, according to the release. 

Nonetheless, the card network giant also plans to increase other fees charged to processors that are typically passed onto merchants, adding a 1.8 cent increase to all domestic transactions in Canada, starting next April, the federation said in the release.

“This is a big win for many small businesses that will now qualify for Visa's special, lower interchange rate,” CFIB President Dan Kelly said in the release. “Sadly, there are new credit card processing fees on the horizon as well.”

Dive Insight:

Back in 2024, San Francisco-based Visa and Purchase, New York-based Mastercard entered into an agreement with the Canadian government agency to reduce interchange fees for small businesses. The reduced interchange rates, under that pact, was for businesses with sales below CA$300,000 when it came to Visa’s fees, and for those with sales below CA$175,000 with respect to Mastercard fees. 

While Visa expanded the program to decrease the interchange fee for more small merchants this month, Mastercard is not changing its program parameters under the pact, per the release. The federation pressed Mastercard to follow its larger rival in expanding the program.

"For two decades, CFIB has been pushing for fairer credit card fees for small businesses,” CFIB executive vice president for advocacy, Corinne Pohlmann, said in the release. “We're glad to see Visa include more small merchants, and we are calling on Mastercard and other card brands to do the same."

Visa confirmed the changes, and a spokesperson said the company aims to provide an average interchange rate of 95 basis points for eligible Canadian small merchants on domestic consumer credit card transactions where a customer is present for the purchase.

“This change will enable more Canadian small businesses to benefit from reduced acceptance costs, reinforcing Visa's commitment to supporting small businesses and expanding digital payments acceptance and strengthening the broader Canadian economy,” the Visa spokesperson said by email.

Mastercard didn’t immediately comment on the changes.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which represents small businesses, has been pushing the government and payment providers to require more credit card providers to participate in its rate-reduction initiative, reassess size limits and secure savings for sellers. 

With respect to the added processor fees, Mastercard started charging the new fee to card processors last week, and Visa will do the same beginning in April 2027, the release said.

The special administrators will gather information from creditors and customers about payments made to, or owed by, EPS and will provide more information on how to make a claim in due course.  

Customers can also contact our Consumer Helpline for more information. 

			

  

      

      						Is the FCA overseeing the special administration?
			
    

    

						

The special administrators are now responsible for EPS, but it continues to be FCA authorised and remains subject to our rules.  The special administrators are officers of the court and must comply with insolvency law.

They have statutory objectives, including engaging with relevant authorities such as the FCA and we will continue working with them during the special administration. 

			

  

      

      						Do I need to use a third party to get my money back? 
			
    

    

						

If you are approached by a company offering to help you recover your money, you should proceed with caution. 

For most of the firm’s clients, there will be no benefit in involving a third party in making a claim.    

If you have any questions about the special administration process, please contact the special administrators using the contact details above.  

			

  

  

            						

Being alert to scams

All customers should remain alert to the possibility of fraud.

If you are contacted unexpectedly by someone claiming to be from EPS, Opus or the FCA, you should end the call and contact them directly using verified contact details.

title: Paze sets big targets after revamp
snippet: The wallet’s bank owners are battling Apple and PayPal with an extensive marketing push, touting it as a more secure payment method.
fullText:
LAS VEGAS – Early Warning Services aims to make inroads with the largest U.S. merchants for its Paze wallet over the next three years after the company revamped its product strategy last year.

Paze is trying to establish a two-sided network with consumers and merchants that embed the digital wallet into their checkout path, much like rival offerings from Apple Pay and PayPal Holdings. Paze’s immediate focus will be on adding the 100 largest U.S. merchants, Early Warning CEO Cameron Fowler said in an interview.

“We’re interested in habituation of high-volume transactions right now,” Fowler said of Paze’s goals, speaking Monday in a hotel suite EWS used for meetings during the Money20/20 financial technology conference this week in Las Vegas. 

A Paze spokesperson had no immediate comment on how many of the top 100 merchants the company has so far. 

Early Warning Services is a consortium owned by seven large U.S. banks, including Bank of America, Capital One Financial and JPMorgan Chase. It also operates the Zelle payments system for bank transfers and Certos, a fraud-prevention and identity risk provider.

Paze has endured a choppy path over the past three years, with slow adoption. 

Serge Elkiner, a former product executive at Visa, joined Early Warning as Paze general manager in October 2024 as part of EWS’s effort to revitalize the project. Elkiner said he realized within a month of joining EWS that the wallet needed a massive overhaul, he said Tuesday in an interview at the conference.

“It was not ready for prime time,” Elkiner said Tuesday, sitting near Paze’s booth on the Money20/20 exhibition floor. The initial Paze wallet had low conversion and approval rates, he said. It was also “not that easy to use because there were too many screens, so we went back to the whiteboard” in May 2025, with a one-year schedule to revamp the wallet, Elkiner said.

Various development milestones were promising during that period, but at the 12-month mark Paze’s conversion and approval rates still weren’t suitable, Elkiner said.

“The power of the consortium is that we can go all the way up to the CEOs if we need to, and we had a heart-to-heart with all the banks, and we said, ‘Guys, we have six weeks because we’re launching 15th of June, and we need to do it, and we need to get the approval rates’” improved, he said. That process also involved working with the major card networks, including Visa and Mastercard, Elkiner added.

To drive Paze usage, the company launched its “It Checks Out” marketing campaign in June, with Hollywood actors Elizabeth Banks and Gabrielle Union playing on their last names to highlight the wallet’s security due to its close ties to banks and credit unions. 

Over the summer, Paze also offered a $10 credit for people who activated Paze on their debit or credit cards and spent at least $10, with the free money allowed for up to 10 transactions per card at specific merchants. Those “Paze craze” deals led people to strategize how to maximize their financial return, with some amassing more than $1,000, Bloomberg reported. The promotion ended Sept. 11.

Paze declined to disclose how much it has spent on the marketing efforts. Elkiner said the company will continue investing on efforts that can expand Paze usage.

“The growth was insane,” Elkiner said of the summer promotional period, with Paze acquiring “a few percentage points of wallet share” in three to six weeks at its merchants due to the free money. “We’re giving money, but we see it works. We see the product is performing, and the performance was really high. We became, at some of our merchants, (the) highest approval rate wallet of all wallets, and that was unheard of. And so the numbers moved.”

Digital wallet competitors include behemoths Apple and PayPal Holdings, along with an upstart in Stripe’s Link, and Android-based wallets from Google and Samsung.

Large merchants that accept Paze include the department store Bloomingdale’s and cosmetics chain Sephora; as well as Dunkin’, the coffee and baked goods chain; and United Airlines.

Paze declined to disclose financial or operating targets for the wallet, but Elkiner said Paze is on track to exceed its 2026 goal for transactions by four times the target.

Paze is targeting a specific group of consumers: Those who aren’t tied to Apple’s ecosystem, people not committed to any particular wallet, and those who trust their bank as a more secure payment provider, Fowler and Elkiner said. That consumer bloc represents 30% to 50% of the market, Fowler said.

Paze has added about 220 million credit and debit cards to the tool, the company said last month in a press release. 

Paze is also spending significantly on sports-oriented marketing, adding its logo last month to the Phoenix Suns’ professional basketball team’s jersey – supplanting rival PayPal in that spot. Paze is already aligned with the Atlanta Hawks basketball team jerseys. It also has announced plans to be a founding partner of Etihad Park in Queens, New York, where soccer club New York City FC will play starting in July 2027.

Paze touts its bank connections as a source of security and notes that it doesn’t share 16-digit card data with merchants, instead tokenizing the information that’s used for payments.

Over time, Paze aims to leverage its reputation as a secure brand backed by banks for people to navigate digital commerce, and avoid sharing data with dozens of websites and wallets, Elkiner said. “The way I look at it is, today I'm a wallet. Tomorrow I'm the access to your secure credential,” he said.

title: New payment rails catch on, slowly
snippet: Some companies have yet to realize the full potential of multi-rail systems, speakers said at the Money20/20 conference Monday.
fullText:
Companies have presided over big shifts in money flows in recent years as technology has transformed transactions. 

Yet speakers at a conference Monday said financial institutions and other businesses will need to overcome more hurdles if they want to realize all of the benefits of instant payments and stablecoins for payment senders and receivers. 

“At the end of the day our customers and their customers are counting on us, they don’t care about the rails, they don’t care about the modality,” Amy Burr, chief product and relationship officer with Federal Reserve Financial Services, said during a panel at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. “They want to know that money is going to move reliably, quickly and independently; the end. That’s the challenge and we need to rise up and meet it.” 

To be sure, businesses are making inroads into new systems. Consumer card-swiping, digital wallets and an ever widening range of corporate payment methods have been part of the transformation of economic exchanges that has driven annual global payments revenue from $1.7 trillion in 2020 to $2.6 trillion last year, according to the consulting firm McKinsey.  

Still, skepticism and old technology are holding some companies and banks back from full adoption of the wider range of alternative forms of the payments — ranging from stablecoins to the Federal Reserve’s instant payment system, FedNow — as well as the benefits that modern payments technology can offer. 

“I spend a fair amount of time talking to financial institutions that just don’t want another thing,” Burr said during the panel discussion at the  conference, noting that some companies are reluctant to add more layers to their technology stack. “The fatigue is real.”

The ideal of a fully activated modernized payments ecosystem and how companies can take steps to surmount the hurdles that are still preventing it from being realized, was the focus of a panel discussion at the annual finance and technology conference.

Burr expressed some skepticism about the uptake of the new technologies because of the relatively lukewarm reception that banks gave to a new international standard known as ISO 20022. The Fedwire Funds Service, which moves trillions of dollars daily, shifted to the standard last year, but banks are just beginning to embrace it and make use of its attributes. 

While there’s been effort to push adoption of the full benefit of ISO 20022, “we’re not really seeing banks and corporates using all the fields so I’m maybe a little pessimistic about programmable money,” Burr said. 

Sam Aarons, CTO of payments software provider Modern Treasury, said he is frustrated personally by capabilities for payments, some of which would make them more user-friendly, but which aren’t being widely adopted. For example, he said he can log into his credit card account and see purchases, but receipts are not included — even though technology can provide that capability and allow card users to have more information about their purchases.  

“It irks me to no end that I can’t log into my American Express portal and see the receipt attached to my payment,” Aarons said, noting that he believes the problem is likely tied to decades old software that hasn’t caught up with technology. “We have all this innovation for stapling context data to payments, and still no one does it.” 

As companies explore their payment system options, Aarons advised that they think about payments rails as a kind of menu, with paths that might or might not fit their needs at a given time. That includes keeping some existing rails operating, such as ACH payments, that some companies like for their low cost, and even paper checks. 

“You still see paper checks; they’re very popular in the United States,” Aarons said. “The volume will get reduced over the years but not to zero.” 

Currently, he said big companies are not viewing stablecoins versus fiat currency as an either or question but are rather using all of them in varied degrees depending on their needs. 

Irfan Ganchi, senior vice president of product management at stablecoin giant Circle Internet Group, agreed. The choice of how the money gets to a place is something that depends on the location of the receivers and senders, as well as the capabilities of the rails, he said. For example, Ganchi said large multinational companies may use stablecoin to move a payment to some of their international entities overnight, but locally they’re going to pay local suppliers and vendors using instant payments. 

“But also there’s an aspect of receiver preference,” he said. “It’s quite possible that a ride sharing driver in Indonesia wants [Circle’s stablecoin] USDC because they want to hold it in dollars. But a ride sharing driver in the U.S. wants dollars or fiat and you have to be able to support both.”  

The Money20/20 conference is owned by Payment Dive’s parent company Informa.

title: Amex to shrink workforce
snippet: The card company plans to cut 4.5% of its employees to become more “agile and efficient” as it adjusts to more use of artificial intelligence, CEO Stephen Squeri said.
fullText:
American Express plans to reduce its headcount by nearly 4.5% as part of a restructuring as competition continues to intensify amid increased industry use of artificial intelligence.

The New York-based card company will cut about 3,500 of its approximately 78,000 workers worldwide, a spokesperson for the company said, in conjunction with announcing its third-quarter earnings report Friday. The spokesperson declined to provide additional details. 

The headcount was higher than the 76,800 workers the company had at the end of last year, according to its annual report.

Amex CEO Stephen Squeri said the workforce contraction was focused on streamlining the company’s operations, bolstering productivity and speeding up decision-making.

“We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become a more agile and efficient organization,” he told analysts on a Friday earnings call.

Company executives on the call provided few additional details about the employee job cuts, other than Squeri explaining how he asked managers this year to identify the options for improving operations.

The move to cut costs comes as competition continues to ramp up. Large banks that issue cards, including JPMorgan Chase, and their card network partners Visa and Mastercard, continue to challenge Amex in the premium consumer card market, with improved loyalty programs and airport lounge offerings.

On the commercial front, new entrants, including Brex and Ramp, are intensifying competition for corporate customers, including with the use of AI agents. Brex was acquired this year by Amex rival bank Capital One, which also completed a purchase of card rival Discover Financial last year.

“Those are two of the big competitors that are out there,” Squeri told analysts on the call in response to a question. “What they unlocked in this segment was sort of the automation and the expense management.” 

“What you'll see from us as we move forward, you will see the introduction into this platform of more agents,” he added.

While there is an opportunity for AI to improve the company’s internal operations, Squeri said, he focused mainly on how AI will be used in the future by customers to consume the company’s services in new ways.

For instance, that technology will allow the company to better personalize restaurant services for its premium customers who make reservations through its partner Resy, tailoring online services to customer’s particular tastes, Squeri said. He also discussed using the AI agent ChatGPT to personalize pitches for Amex’s restaurant and travel services.

Overall, demand from the company’s card customers, which historically have tended to be more affluent, is healthy, the company’s executives told analysts on the call. 

Amex’s billed business rose 8% to $454 billion for the quarter, on a foreign-exchange adjusted basis, over the year-earlier quarter, the company reported. Still, that was down from 9% for the first half of the year, according to the company’s earnings presentation.

“Strong and consistent” is how the company’s chief financial officer, Christophe Le Caillec, described the current customer demand.

Amex third-quarter net income jumped 28% to $3.71 billion as the company’s revenue rose 9% to $20 billion, according to the Friday earnings press release. 

In addition to the $336 million charge during the quarter associated with restructuring, the company had a gain from the sale of the company’s travel services business this year and took account of a penalty the company was forced to pay to settle an enforcement action brought by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. That $350 million fine was due to the bank’s alleged failures to follow anti-money laundering regulations.

Overall, the company’s expenses rose 9% to $14.5 billion, including an 11% increase in spending for marketing, according to the earnings presentation.

Amex is seeking to bolster its position with lower-income customers too by partnering with companies, such as Bread Financial and Synchrony, but it will avoid partnering with the big-bank rivals on that front because those alliances didn’t work out in the past, Squeri said.

“It's allowing us to reach more segments of the population that we traditionally wouldn't reach,” Squeri said of working with companies like Bread Financial and Synchrony. “We will continue to see, I believe, more and more of those deals be done.”
